- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
The woman from the sound archive asked us to turn off the refrigerator.

“How long?” my father said.

“Three minutes.”

“It takes longer than that to get cold again.”

She looked at me. I unplugged it.

Our house was one of forty-six being knocked down for the new flood channel. The county had offered each household a truck, six months’ storage, and a recording of one room. My father had turned down the truck because he owned a truck, turned down the storage because he didn’t believe it would be dry, and accepted the recording because he wanted to see how anybody could make a recording of a room with nobody talking in it.

The woman’s name was Ruth. She had a small microphone with a fur cover. My father asked if she had to brush it.

“Sometimes,” she said, and showed him the comb.

He liked her after that.

We had chosen the kitchen. Or rather, I had written *kitchen* on the form while my father was in the garage finding a pen. I’d spent the previous two weekends packing that room. At the back of the junk drawer I’d found eleven keys, some gray birthday candles, and a note in my own childhood handwriting that said PLEASE BUY PEARS. On the reverse, my father had written a tire size. I put it in the box with the cutlery rather than try to decide whose rubbish it was.

Ruth set up the microphone by the bread bin. She told us we could stay as long as we sat still.

“What if a car goes by?” my father asked.

“Then we’ll have the car.”

“What if the phone rings?”

“Does it often?”

“Not anymore,” he said.

Ruth started the recorder.

For the first few seconds I could only hear my own breathing. Then there was a tick above the stove, where the clock had been. My father had taken it down that morning. I looked up anyway; there was a round patch of clean wall and, through the wall, a small intermittent ticking I’d apparently been giving the clock credit for all my life.

A car went by.

My father sat with his hands flat on his knees. At seventy-four he still had the forearms of somebody who could carry a washing machine with one other man. He had been offered a ground-floor apartment near a bakery. He’d taken it, then complained that the bedroom window looked onto the bakery’s loading bay. When I pointed out that the trucks would come early, he said he knew when trucks came. He’d driven one for thirty-eight years.

His route used to bring him home at four in the morning. When I was little I would wake to the hinge on the back door, then the kettle, then the click of the teaspoon he set down on the counter. Some mornings I padded out and sat with him. He let me dunk toast in his tea, although he objected to the crumbs.

When I was twelve I began staying in bed. I could hear the hinge, the kettle, the teaspoon, and sometimes his steps coming as far as my door. He never knocked. At the time I thought this was evidence that we understood each other.

Somewhere in the second minute my father’s chair creaked. His eyes went to Ruth. She shook her head a little to say it was fine.

When the three minutes were up, she put headphones on him first. I watched him listen. Halfway through, he lifted one ear cup.

“Is that me?”

“The chair?” Ruth said. “Yes.”

“No, before.”

She backed up the recording. He listened again, then handed me the headphones.

At first there was just the soft, steady sound of the room. Then I heard myself take two short breaths close together, almost a sniff.

“You used to do that,” he said. “Before you came out.”

I took off the headphones. “You could hear me from the kitchen?”

“Not from the kitchen.”

Ruth began winding a cable around her hand.

“I thought you were asleep most of the time,” my father said. “But then I’d hear that and put another piece of bread in.”

I tried to remember whether, on the mornings I’d stayed in bed, he’d come to my door before or after he made his toast. I could remember the stripe of light under the door, and how I used to move one foot into it and take it out again.

“Did you eat both pieces?” I asked.

“Usually.”

Ruth gave us a card with a link on it. My father turned it over, looking for the rest of the instructions, and I told him I’d put the file on his phone. He walked her out to her car. Through the window I saw him stop her before she drove off. He had remembered the comb, which she’d left next to the bread bin.

I plugged the refrigerator back in. It shuddered and settled into a hum so familiar I hadn’t noticed it was gone.

My father came in and asked if I was staying for lunch. I’d said earlier that I couldn’t. I had a call at one, and if I left now I could make it from my own desk, with the door shut and all my papers where I wanted them. I texted to ask if we could do it at two.

“There’s not much,” he said, looking in the refrigerator we’d spent the week emptying. “I could make toast.”

I took two plates out of the box. He put the bread in and pushed down the lever. Before the toast came up he pushed it down a second time, because it was an old toaster and that was what you had to do. I’d forgotten. I stood there while he did it, holding the plates, though there was a clear place on the counter where I could have put them down.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet literary story built around a father and child recording the sounds of a home before it is demolished.

## Grounded reading
The voice is restrained and observant, letting small physical details carry the emotion: a ticking behind the wall, a teaspoon, two breaths, toast pushed down twice. Its pathos comes from a belated recognition that father and child had been attending to each other without quite saying so. The narrator’s childhood belief that silence meant mutual understanding gives way to a more tender, specific discovery: her father heard her waking and made extra toast. The story invites the reader to notice how care can persist in habits and sounds after the people involved have stopped naming it.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds a home being displaced by a flood channel, the sounds that make a room familiar, and the ordinary objects left between generations: keys, a handwritten note, a clock, a comb, bread, and a toaster. It gives special weight to listening and to missed or delayed communication, while resolving the scene not through a grand declaration but through the narrator staying for lunch and holding the plates.

## Evidence line
> I plugged the refrigerator back in.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The story’s coherent network of sound, domestic objects, and understated care makes its emotional emphasis distinctive and sustained within the sample.
